A group of six students worked on an investigation on flood risk around the Punggol Waterway which flows through the Punggol Waterway Park and Punggol residential estate. The Punggol Waterway connects the Serangoon River in the east to the Punggol River in the west. These three bodies of waters are dammed to create the Punggol- Serangoon Reservoir. They selected two sites X and Y along the Punggol Waterway for their investigation.
Their hypothesis is that flood risk is higher in built-up areas relative to vegetated areas.

To assess the flood risk of the Punggol Waterway Park and Punggol residential estate, they collect data on infiltration rates and selected river variables. They collected data on a weekend in November from 9 am to 4 pm. At each site, two students worked on the infiltration test, while four worked on collecting data on selected river variables. All six of them worked at site X, and then then moved onto site Y after lunch.

For infiltration, the students chose a location at each site, as shown in Resource 2. The equipment used included an infiltrometer made of white plastic tubing with a diameter of 10 cm and a height of 30 cm. The infiltrometer was hammered into the ground using a pebble found nearby. A student used a pail to fetch water from the river for the infiltration test. Water was poured to the top of the infiltrometer, and using a stopwatch, the water level dropping in the infiltrometer was read every 5 minutes. When water reached the base of the infiltrometer, water was poured into the infiltrometer again.
For the river variables, the following data were collected:
• Channel width – Two students on the footbridge that span the river at each site used a tape measure to stretch across the bridge to measure the river width from above.

• Channel depth – This was obtained by extending a long nylon string with a plumb bob (weight) from the bridge at regular intervals of 5 metres across the span of the footbridge from one river to the opposite bank. The plumb bob was lowered into the river to touch the river bed, and the river depth was obtained by measuring the length of the string and the plumb bob.
• River velocity – This was measured using a floating orange to travel a 5-metre distance along the river. Velocity readings were taken once at each site.

There are plans to turn the coastal mangrove area around the Sungai Mandai Besar River in northern Singapore into a nature park that will be named the Mandai Mangrove & Mudflat Nature Park. A group of five students wanted to assess the flood risk around the Sungai Mandai Besar River. The river is concretised into a canal for most of its course except for the short stretch at the river mouth.
The hypothesis the students chose:
‘Fluvial flood risk is lower near the river mouth than around the canalised parts of the Sungai Mandai Besar River.’
To assess the flood risk of the areas surrounding the river, the students collected data on infiltration rates and selected river variables.

They collected data on a weekday in December from 10 am to 4 pm. At each site, two students worked on the infiltration test, while three worked on collecting data on selected river variables. All five of them worked at Site A first. They were only able to start work at Site B after the thunderstorm ended at 3 pm. They collected infiltration data around Site B, and only the river velocity data at Site B.

• A single-ring infiltrometer made of white plastic tubing with a diameter of 10 cm and a height of 30 cm
• Two brightly marked half-filled plastic mineral water bottles as the velocity-floats
• Two stop watches
• A pail to fetch water from the river for the infiltration test

For the infiltration test, the students chose two locations at each site. At Site A, the infiltration test was taken at the grassy patch next to the river bank (indicated as A1 in Resource 1) and on forested land (indicated as A2). At Site B, two infiltration sites were chosen [indicated as B1 (concrete surface) and B2 (muddy river banks) in Resource 1].

The students’ key geographical question was: “How can the inadequacies of road safety measures in housing estates in Singapore be improved to enhance safety for the elderly?”.

To explore this, they first conducted secondary research on the locations where road safety measures had been put in place to cater to the needs of the elderly. This initiative by the Land Transport Authority (LTA) aims to make daily journeys to key amenities in neighbourhoods safer, more convenient and comfortable for those walking or cycling.

A group of four students wanted to investigate the effectiveness of the Beverage Container Return Scheme (BCRS) in encouraging recycling habits amongst residents in Bishan. The BCRS is a national recycling programme where used plastic beverage containers can be returned to reverse vending machines, known as Return Right reverse vending machines, in exchange for a 10-cent deposit refund. The scheme aims to reduce plastic waste and support climate change mitigation efforts.
The hypothesis for their investigation was:
"The greater the convenience of recycling, the more likely that residents in Bishan will engage in recycling behaviours."

After secondary research, the students decided to conduct their investigation at Block 512 in Bishan, where a "Return Right" reverse vending machine is in front of a supermarket, and neighbouring blocks. They conducted their data collection on a Friday afternoon between 3:00 pm and 5:00 pm.
One student was stationed near the reverse vending machine at Block 512 for the 2-hour duration to conduct a pedestrian count and observe the utilisation of the reverse vending machine.

The remaining three students positioned themselves separately at various locations in the vicinity of the reverse vending machine and used convenience sampling to approach passers-by to complete a questionnaire survey. The questionnaire survey focused on their use of the reverse vending machine and their recycling habits. At the end of the 2-hour period, they had surveyed a total of 48 participants. They focused on factors affecting the physical wellbeing of the elderly in East Austin, a neighbourhood in Austin, Texas. The research question was:
‘Has rising heat affected the physical wellbeing of elderly residents, aged 65 and above, living in East Austin?’

A group of four students conducted fieldwork to understand fluvial flood risk in Kuantan Town, Malaysia. They wanted to examine whether certain areas along the river experience different levels of flooding during the monsoon season.
The students selected two sites along public esplanades - Site A at Esplanade Kuantan and Site B at Esplanade Tanjung Api.

Their investigation focused on testing the hypothesis: ‘The Esplanade Kuantan area (Site A) has a higher flood risk than Esplanade Tanjung Api (Site B) due to differences in urban development along the river.’
For each site, they created a grid of twenty-five 20m x 20m squares covering an area extending 100m from the river's edge. Using Google Earth imagery, they classified each grid square as either:
• Built-up: Areas covered by buildings, roads, and paved surfaces
• Recreational space: Parks, sports facilities, and landscaped areas
• Natural surface: Undeveloped areas with trees, shrubs, or grass

During their field survey, the students used the public walkways at both sites to collect data. Using measuring tapes, they recorded the distance between the river's edge and the nearest buildings. They also noted the riverbank characteristics and measured the width of public walkways. All measurements were taken between 9am and 11am on a weekday to ensure consistency.

A group of four students conducted fieldwork to investigate how a community living in the Red River Delta, Vietnam, is responding to increased flood risk associated with climate change. They wanted to examine whether residents in the area were adequately prepared for the more frequent and severe flooding that the region has experienced in recent years.
The students conducted their investigation at Giao Lạc, a low-lying fishing village close to the mouth of the Red River. The village has experienced notable flooding in three of the past five years.
Their investigation focused on testing the hypothesis: 'Most residents in the village have a low level of flood preparedness despite experiencing increased flooding in recent years.'
To collect data, the students spent approximately four hours at the village on a single afternoon.

They conducted a focus group discussion with eight adult residents. They used a set of questions to assess their awareness of flood risk, experience of past flood events, and knowledge of emergency procedures. The students took turns leading different sections of the discussion, with two students recording responses by hand while the other two observed and added supplementary notes. Eight students undertook an investigation into access to heat-relief facilities in Chinatown, Boston City, Massachusetts, USA. These facilities are established and managed by local community organisations. They examined the relationship between heat exposure and access to heat-relief facilities by investigating the hypothesis:
“Residents of Boston Chinatown living in areas of greater heat exposure have better access to heat-relief facilities.”
They selected four residential sites A, B, C and D, within Boston Chinatown. They collected data between 1.00 p.m. and 3.00 p.m. on a weekday in July, during the summer period.

Two students were assigned to each site. At their assigned site, they measured air temperature using a digital thermometer and estimated the percentage of shade cover. Both students then walked separately from their respective sites to the nearest heat-relief facility, and their recorded walking times were added together and divided by two to obtain the mean walking time. They also conducted a questionnaire survey with the first 10 adult respondents at each site who were available and willing to participate, asking about their perceived accessibility of heat-relief facilities.

Four 17-year old students undertook an investigation about the perception of consumers of community responses to climate change in Singapore. They examined the perception of consumers by investigating the hypothesis -
‘Consumers in Singapore see a stronger role for community response than for government and businesses in tackling climate change.’
Community response was defined as ‘any action carried out by non-governmental and non-corporate stakeholders’.

The students collected primary data by conducting a survey in May and did so by asking their friends to participate in an online survey and sought their help to forward the link to family and friends. When they were unable to reach their targeted sample size of 100 respondents, the students decided to expand their number of responses for the survey by conducting the survey individually outside a busy shopping mall - Bugis Junction - on a Wednesday and Thursday afternoon. Passers-by were approached to do the survey.
